Presidential races traditionally start in Iowa, where the state’s caucuses often produce bustling, energetic—and sometimes confusing—outcomes. It’s the beautiful backdrop of early political euphoria.

   Novembers in Iowa don’t traditionally bring as much drama. 

   Republicans in recent years have tightened their hold on the state, controlling the governor’s mansion since 2011 and holding both U.S. Senate seats since 2015.

   That could be about to change.

   The margins in Iowa’s race for governor and one U.S. Senate seat are looking razor thin, according to polls.

   GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are locked in a tight duel for the Senate.

   Similarly, Republican Zach Lahn appears to be slightly trailing Democrat Rob Sand to become the state’s next governor. 

   One big question is: Why?

   Rising energy prices are affecting everyone, but energy issues tend to hit harder in Iowa, where agriculture and ethanol are central to many livelihoods. 

   Vulnerable Iowa GOP incumbents have broken with President Trump on the Iran war, reflecting this dynamic (energy prices are higher because of the war).

   So watch Iowa on election night. If it’s closer than in years past, or if Democrats somehow find a way to break through, that could tell us a lot about 2026 and the mood heading into 2028. It could also set up the narrative for the presidential races early, as the state might feel like it’s in play for the first time in quite a while. If Republicans hold on to the Senate seat and the governorship, the GOP candidates might have deftly positioned themselves in a way to avoid some of the broader national crosscurrents.

High Energy Prices Give Democrats Hope of an Unusual Breakthrough in Iowa
 
Plus, lawmakers want colleagues to promise to accept election results, and what six years of inflation means for the midterms
 
 
CHARLIE NEIBERGALL/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. Presidential races traditionally start in Iowa, where the state’s caucuses often produce bustling, energetic—and sometimes confusing—outcomes. It’s the beautiful backdrop of early political euphoria.

 

Novembers in Iowa don’t traditionally bring as much drama. 

 

Republicans in recent years have tightened their hold on the state, controlling the governor’s mansion since 2011 and holding both U.S. Senate seats since 2015.

 

That could be about to change.

 

The margins in Iowa’s race for governor and one U.S. Senate seat are looking razor thin, according to polls.

 

GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are locked in a tight duel for the Senate.

 

Similarly, Republican Zach Lahn appears to be slightly trailing Democrat Rob Sand to become the state’s next governor. 

 

One big question is: Why?

 

Rising energy prices are affecting everyone, but energy issues tend to hit harder in Iowa, where agriculture and ethanol are central to many livelihoods. 

 

Vulnerable Iowa GOP incumbents have broken with President Trump on the Iran war, reflecting this dynamic (energy prices are higher because of the war).

 

So watch Iowa on election night. If it’s closer than in years past, or if Democrats somehow find a way to break through, that could tell us a lot about 2026 and the mood heading into 2028. It could also set up the narrative for the presidential races early, as the state might feel like it’s in play for the first time in quite a while. If Republicans hold on to the Senate seat and the governorship, the GOP candidates might have deftly positioned themselves in a way to avoid some of the broader national crosscurrents.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Michigan debate: Michigan Senate candidates—Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed—will have their first debate this evening.

 

Dr. Erica Schwartz: The CDC’s new director aims to change a culture of “paternalism” at the agency as she faces a number of challenges in her first months.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president’s schedule for today hasn’t been released as of the time of this newsletter’s publication.

What I’m Following

 
 
JOE LAMBERTI/GETTY IMAGES
 

Lawmakers want their colleagues to promise they will accept election results. Democrats and anti-Trump Republicans are anxious that the current GOP-controlled Congress could thwart the seating of Democrats in January. A bipartisan group of lawmakers is trying to take the tactic off the table, asking for written pledges from their colleagues to accept the midterm-election results.

 

What six years of inflation means for the midterms. Most voters don’t really care (or know) that the inflation rate is 3.4%, but they do care that over the past five years the price of coffee has more than doubled and the cost of beef has shot up 50%. While some Americans have seen their wages keep up, the sticky psychology of prices mean that few have mentally adjusted to a world where the per-pound price of chicken starts with a 2, not a 1.

 

The U.S.’s ambassador to Greece pushed a MAGA donor to wire money to her Amex account. Kimberly Guilfoyle had offered Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate in Kentucky, access to top administration officials ahead of her confirmation as ambassador. Deters didn’t ultimately make the $100,000 payment, but the back and forth raises new questions about the activities of one of America’s most high-profile ambassadors.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats would move swiftly to reverse Trump-era cuts to healthcare spending and bring down households’ costs should his party win a majority in November.

 

• U.S. forces in Okinawa face a curfew and alcohol ban after a marine was accused of killing a Japanese woman.

 

• Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is now the biggest in the U.S. in 35 years.
